interviewQuestions.question: Why is Linux monolithic and Minix a microkernel — what's the trade-off?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd frame this as two different priorities, not one design being objectively better. Linux was built to be a fast, general-purpose Unix for real machines — Linus Torvalds explicitly optimized for performance, putting the scheduler, filesystems, network stack, and drivers all in kernel space so they call each other directly with no IPC tax.

Minix was built by Andrew Tanenbaum primarily as a teaching and research OS, later evolving toward high reliability — it pushes drivers and filesystems into user-space servers so a crash in one doesn't take down the kernel, accepting IPC overhead for that guarantee. This is literally the subject of the famous Tanenbaum-Torvalds debate in the early 1990s, where each defended their priority.

The trade-off in one line: monolithic buys you speed by giving up isolation; microkernel buys you isolation by giving up some speed. I'd close by noting Minix 3 actually achieved real fault tolerance this way — it can restart a crashed driver transparently, something Linux can't do for a crashed built-in driver.

**Testing:** whether you understand this as a deliberate trade-off with real historical context, not just a definitional fact to recite.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Linux vs Minix, the classic debate

interviewQuestions.question: If microkernels are more fault-tolerant, why doesn't a mainstream OS like Linux just switch to one?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd point out this isn't really a hypothetical — it's been tried and the economics didn't favor a full switch. The core issue is that decades of Linux's performance, driver ecosystem, and application compatibility are built on monolithic assumptions (direct function calls, shared kernel address space); a rewrite to a microkernel architecture would mean re-engineering essentially the entire driver and subsystem ecosystem for a performance regression on the common path, in exchange for a benefit (isolation) that most Linux workloads don't strictly require.

Instead, Linux has taken an incremental path: FUSE lets specific filesystems run in user space when isolation matters more than raw speed for that use case, without touching the rest of the kernel's architecture. This gets some of the microkernel benefit surgically, where it's worth the cost, rather than paying the IPC tax everywhere.

I'd also flag that the workloads that most need microkernel-level isolation — safety-critical, security-critical systems — already have purpose-built options like seL4 rather than needing Linux to become one.

**Testing:** whether you can reason about a large-scale engineering trade-off in terms of migration cost and incremental alternatives, not just "microkernels are better, why not switch."
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why mainstream OSes stay monolithic

interviewQuestions.question: What's the difference between a hybrid kernel and a monolithic kernel with loadable modules? Aren't they basically the same thing?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd distinguish them by what the split is based on, not just how flexible each is. A monolithic kernel with loadable modules (Linux) is architecturally one big kernel — modules are just a runtime-loading mechanism for code that still runs with full, undifferentiated kernel privilege, with no conceptual separation between subsystems beyond source-code organization.

A hybrid kernel (Windows NT, XNU) is explicitly structured around subsystem boundaries inspired by microkernel design — even though it runs most of them in kernel space for speed, the architecture itself reflects a deliberate, documented split (XNU literally combines a distinct Mach layer with a distinct BSD layer, each with its own APIs and historical lineage).

So the practical difference is intent and structure, not runtime privilege: LKMs are a monolithic kernel's answer to flexibility without isolation; hybrid kernels are a structural compromise that borrows microkernel-style organization while keeping monolithic-style performance for the pieces that need it.

**Testing:** whether you can tell the difference between a mechanism (loadable modules) and an architectural philosophy (hybrid design), since they're easy to conflate.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Hybrid kernel vs monolithic-with-modules

interviewQuestions.question: How would you decide between a monolithic-style and microkernel-style approach when designing a new embedded system?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd start by asking what a component failure actually costs in this system. If it's a consumer device where a crashed subsystem means an annoying reboot, I'd lean monolithic or hybrid — the performance and simpler engineering are worth it, and the failure mode is tolerable.

If it's something where a failure has real safety or financial consequences — a medical device, an automotive control unit, industrial equipment — I'd lean toward a microkernel-style design specifically because it lets me isolate the riskiest, least-trusted components (say, a network stack processing untrusted input) into restartable, contained services, even at real IPC cost.

I'd also factor in team and ecosystem reality: a full microkernel is harder to develop for and has fewer existing drivers, so for many embedded projects a pragmatic middle ground — a small trusted core plus a couple of isolated high-risk components (a real-world RTOS-plus-sandboxed-subsystem pattern) — often beats either pure extreme.

**Testing:** whether you can apply the trade-off to a concrete design decision instead of only explaining it in the abstract.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Applying the trade-off to a new design
